card.hook: You can't drive to Railay. You need a boat, and that's the first sign you're in for a good day. Then you step onto Ao Phra Nang and get pale sand, calm water, a tall cliff and a little island, all in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand mid-beach on the sand at Ao Phra Nang (Phra Nang Beach). Face the limestone cliffs and the little island, Ko Rang Nok, just offshore.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the cliffs, sand and sea in together. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Ko Rang Nok or a passing longtail boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and put the horizon on a lower line so the cliffs fill the top of the frame.
card.best_time: Go before 9 AM if you can. The light reaches the cliffs by then and the beach is much quieter.
card.selfie_here: For a big-view selfie, try the Bat Cave photo ledge above Phra Nang Cave Beach. Use the front camera at 0.5x and the whole bay stretches out behind you. You get there by a bamboo ladder and a dark cave opening, so it's not a casual stroll.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sand facing the huge overhanging cliff at the south end of Phra Nang Beach, so the cliff and beach fit in one frame, and you stand in front of it.
card.rules_and_safety: The Bat Cave and Railay Viewpoint climbs are steep and slippery, and guides say they become dangerous after rain, so wear proper footwear and skip the Viewpoint hike during or right after rain. Selfie sticks are listed as allowed on the beach, but that info is a few years old, so check locally.
card.challenge: Snap a longtail boat gliding past with your horizon sitting neatly on a gridline. Bonus points if you get Ko Rang Nok in the same shot.
card.good_to_know: Railay is a small peninsula cut off from the mainland by high limestone cliffs, which is why you can only reach it by boat. Its cliffs draw rock climbers from around the world, and it has been a popular Krabi beach destination since tourism began there in the 1970s. Ao Phra Nang is one of four main areas, alongside West Railay, East Railay and Ton Sai.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand mid-beach on the sand at Ao Phra Nang (Phra Nang Beach). Face the limestone cliffs and the little island, Ko Rang Nok, just offshore.

card.hook: Down on the sand, Ao Nang is just a beach. From up here it's the whole show at once, with limestone mountains behind and the sea and beaches stacked in layers below.
card.stand_here: Stand at Ao Nang Viewpoint, the roadside lookout on the road between Ao Nang and Nopparat Thara, about 500 m before Nopparat Thara. There's roadside parking, so face out over the Ao Nang area below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the mountains, beaches and sea together. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out the limestone peaks or the boats on the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, then tap the sky and slide it a little darker so the sunset colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Sunset, roughly 5:30 to 6:30 p.m., is the time to aim for. Get there a bit early to claim a spot and take a few frames as the light changes.
card.selfie_here: For the classic Krabi shot, head to the big rocks at the south end of Ao Nang Beach and pose on the boulders with the limestone mountain rising behind you. Go at 6:30-7:30 a.m. or at sunset, use the front camera at 0.5x, and keep the mountain over your shoulder. The steel sailfish statue on the beach promenade, facing the sea, makes a good second selfie backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the roadside parking area to stand on the roadside side, while you stand at the edge with the town and bay spread out below you.
card.rules_and_safety: Pull over only where it is safe, and respect private property. Check access to the viewpoint locally before you set out.
card.challenge: Zoom in and spot a long-tail boat crossing the water far below. Bonus points if you can follow it for a few seconds.
card.good_to_know: Ao Nang is one of the ten subdistricts of Mueang Krabi District. Its main street is packed with restaurants, pubs and shops aimed at tourists. Long-tail boats run from the main beach to other beaches and nearby islands, and the viewpoint is described as free to visit.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Ao Nang Viewpoint, the roadside lookout on the road between Ao Nang and Nopparat Thara, about 500 m before Nopparat Thara. There's roadside parking, so face out over the Ao Nang area below.

selfie_research.notes: Ao Nang is a whole town and bay rather than a single landmark, so 'landmark behind' is my interpretation: the sources describe the mountain or sea behind the spots rather than Ao Nang town itself. The passer-by spot is inferred from a viewpoint that overlooks the whole Ao Nang area, so the town would appear behind the visitor only if the photographer stands on the roadside side of the viewpoint. card.hook: A monkey strolls through your photo like it's got a reservation, and a 1,260-step staircase waits behind it. Welcome to Tiger Cave Temple, where the backdrop does half the work for you.
card.stand_here: At Tiger Cave Temple (Wat Tham Suea), stand about 90 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the temple. Take your first frames here before you walk on.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the temple buildings and statues, then try 0.5x to fit in the mountains, trees and buildings together. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details, and for monkeys from a safe distance.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the golden statue, then slide the brightness a little darker so the gold keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning is a sensible choice, since the climb is likely cooler and the crowds smaller. If you reach the north-west stupa at the summit early, you may get a warm golden-hour glow. Check the official site for current opening arrangements.
card.selfie_here: At the top of the stairs, stand beside the giant golden Buddha with the valley and Krabi view behind it. Use the front camera at 0.5x and tilt up slightly so Buddha and view both squeeze in. The north-west stupa at the summit is another early-light spot, so check both on arrival.
card.ask_someone: At the foot of the stairway, stand by the start-of-steps sign with the stairs rising behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot so the staircase and temple both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed, but respect any signs that prohibit photos in certain areas. Dress modestly, covering knees and shoulders, and take your shoes off before stepping onto the tiled temple area at the summit. Monkeys are around the grounds, so don't feed or approach them, as they can be unpredictable.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the stairs with a monkey in the frame (a safe distance away, please) and one of you looking suitably triumphant at the top.
card.good_to_know: The temple dates back to 1975, when a monk went to meditate in the cave and saw tigers roaming around it. That's how the place got its name, and the cave is known for its tiger paw prints. The stairway has 1,260 steps up to 278 metres, and some risers are over 30 cm high, so stop and shoot on the way up rather than saving it all for the top.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: At Tiger Cave Temple (Wat Tham Suea), stand about 90 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east towards the temple. Take your first frames here before you walk on.

card.hook: Serpents line both sides of the staircase, and they're pointing you up a hill in the middle of Krabi Town. Climb it, then do what most people forget: turn around.
card.stand_here: Stand on the hilltop terrace at the top of the naga staircase, right at the phone icon on the map. Face away from the white hall, looking back over the town toward the river.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the big town view. Tap 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out rooftops and the river. Save 0.5x for the staircase, when you want all the nagas in one shot.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper third line, then tap the town or river and slide a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the sweet spot, when the sunset light softens the hills and the town. It also makes the climb feel like a reward.
card.selfie_here: Take it on the upper terrace just past the top of the naga staircase. Use the front camera at 0.5x, face out over the town roofs and keep the white temple buildings behind your shoulder. For a second one, stand on the lower steps holding the golden naga balustrade, facing down the stairs with the temple above you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the street side of Maharat Road, opposite Vogue Mall, facing the entrance staircase, while you stand on the lower steps by the naga rails. Check the frame on the spot, since the temple may sit right at the top edge.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so dress modestly and follow the posted rules. Photos are generally fine on the terrace and in the grounds, but the ordination hall has restrictions, and signs at the entrance say no professional photo shoots. The steps can be slippery when wet, so wear shoes with a good grip.
card.challenge: Get one shot of the river with rooftops filling the frame, then one of the naga staircase from Maharat Road. See if the two look like they belong to the same trip.
card.good_to_know: Wat Kaew Korawaram is a Buddhist temple on a hill above downtown Krabi Town, and one of the larger temples in the area. It's less famous than Wat Tham Suea (Tiger Cave Temple). You reach it from an entrance plaza off one of the town's main streets, then climb the staircase to the white ordination hall at the top.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the hilltop terrace at the top of the naga staircase, right at the phone icon on the map. Face away from the white hall, looking back over the town toward the river.

selfie_spots.why: The terrace is described as a large open area with the white temple buildings on one side and views over the town, so a selfie facing outward keeps the temple behind you.

selfie_research.safety: The steps are manageable but can be slippery when wet, so wear well-gripped footwear.
selfie_research.notes: No page I found states a selfie stick or tripod rule for this temple, so none is listed. One page says photography is generally permitted on the terrace and in the gardens but asks for discretion inside the ordination hall, and another says professional photo shoots are not permitted per a sign at the entrance; these are photography rules, not selfie stick or tripod rules, so I left them out as instructed. The sources disagree on the staircase: one says about 100 steps, another describes 8 flights of 8 steps, and a third says it is only a couple of minutes' climb. The first selfie spot is the top terrace, not the staircase alone. The 'ask someone' spot is across the road, so the stairs are shot from below and the temple sits above the frame's top edge; no page confirms that exact framing, so check it on the spot.

card.hook: Picture a curve of pale sand, a cliff straight out of a postcard, and longtail boats bobbing like they were hired for the shot. Phra Nang Beach has no road to it, so you've already earned the view before you take the photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on Railay Viewpoint, the hilltop lookout on the trail between Phra Nang Beach and Railay East, and look south-west over Phra Nang Beach. It's a steep, unmarked climb of about 25 minutes with a scramble and a squeeze through a tunnel, so wear closed shoes and keep your phone in your pocket on the way up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the beach, Railay East and Railay West into one frame. Then try 1x for a calmer view, and 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the cliffs, the rock islet or the longtail boats.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the curve of the beach along a lower line and let the limestone cliffs fill the top. Tap the brightest part of the sky or water, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the pale sand doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Check the tide before you go. One guide says the beach may not be visible at high tide, while another recommends high tide for the Bat Cave view, so pick the shot you want first.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie, try the Bat Cave viewpoint at the west end of the beach. Stand where the narrow tunnel opens out, use the front camera and let the beach sit behind you. Or stand in front of the Princess Cave shrine grotto on the cliff-shaded left side of the beach, and the beach and cliffs will be behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: At low tide, ask someone to wander out onto the small peninsula on Phra Nang Beach for a wide shot of you and the cliffs, while you stand on the beach facing them (the exact spot is approximate).
card.rules_and_safety: The Bat Cave is also a rock-climbing area, so keep out of climbers' way. If you wade out to the island at low tide, watch for sharp stones and coral. The viewpoint climb is tough, so skip it if it sounds like too much.
card.challenge: Take the same shot at 0.5x, 1x and 2x, then see which one makes you say 'wow' the loudest.
card.good_to_know: Phra Nang Beach is in the Railay area of Krabi, next to Railay East and Railay West. Boats land at Railay, and the last stretch is a walk of about 10 minutes from Railay East. If the climb is too much, the beach is a gentler option, or you can use the Bat Cave opening as a natural frame onto the beach and Ko Rang Nok island.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Railay Viewpoint, the hilltop lookout on the trail between Phra Nang Beach and Railay East, and look south-west over Phra Nang Beach. It's a steep, unmarked climb of about 25 minutes with a scramble and a squeeze through a tunnel, so wear closed shoes and keep your phone in your pocket on the way up.

selfie_research.notes: No page found states rules on selfie sticks or tripods, so none are listed. The ask-someone spot is described only as 'the small peninsula' with no exact name, and no page says which way the photographer should face, so the position is approximate. The Bat Cave and shrine selfie spots are sourced from guides that describe the views but do not explicitly say where to pose. The Princess Cave shrine is a feature of the beach rather than the beach itself, so it is included as a near-landmark spot. The Bat Cave viewpoint is on the west end and reached by a jungle path with ladders, so it is not a casual stop.

card.hook: Picture white sand under your toes, turquoise water in the middle, and one giant limestone rock sticking out of the sea like it's waiting for its close-up. That's Ko Poda's northeast beach, and it really is the classic holiday photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sand of the northeast beach, right where the phone icon sits, because you're already at the subject and there's no extra walk. Face the big limestone rock out in the sea in front of the island.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the curve of the sand and the whole height of the rock. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural look. For the rock's texture, step back and use 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) instead of walking closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on a lower or upper third line, and place the rock off-centre so the curve of the shoreline leads your eye to it.
card.best_time: Sunset is the best moment, with the sun going down behind the rock formation. Tour groups fill the beach from late morning until about 1-2 pm, so early or late gives you cleaner shots with fewer people in them.
card.selfie_here: On the beach, use the front camera at 0.5x and turn around so the big rock sits over your shoulder. For a bonus, Chicken Island Viewpoint is on Koh Kai, a neighbouring island. It's a short climb up the hill opposite the sandbank to Tub Island, and Koh Poda sits behind you in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a beach on an island reached by boat, so check with your tour operator or the official site for access, boat times and any fees before you go.
card.challenge: Find a patch of wet sand and use it as your foreground, with the shoreline curving off towards the rock. Bonus points if a wave rolls in during a Live Photo.
card.good_to_know: Ko Poda is a small island just off the Krabi coast. The same northeast beach is also described as the best place on the island to swim, so you can pair your photos with a dip. If you want somewhere quieter, Secret Beach is a small bay with rock cliffs on both sides, reached only by boat.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sand of the northeast beach, right where the phone icon sits, because you're already at the subject and there's no extra walk. Face the big limestone rock out in the sea in front of the island.

selfie_spots.name: Chicken Island Viewpoint (on Koh Kai)
selfie_spots.detail: up the small hill opposite the sandbank to Tub Island, reached by a short climb
selfie_spots.why: Opposite the sandbank to Tub Island, there is a small climb up the hill that leads to Chicken Island Viewpoint. This Krabi viewpoint offers a beautiful view of Tub Island and Koh Poda in the background, so Koh Poda sits behind you in the frame.

sources.title: Krabi Viewpoints - The 8 Most Beautiful Views

selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is supported by a page. It is on Koh Kai (Chicken Island), a neighbouring island, not on Koh Poda, and rests on a single source. No page I found gave a standing point for a passer-by to photograph a visitor with the whole Koh Poda landmark in view, so ask_someone_spot is null. Other Poda photo locations (the mast-shaped limestone 'Hin Poda' in front of the island, and the Ma Tang Ming reef shot taken with a longtail boat) were named by a trip guide, but the pages do not say where the visitor stands with Koh Poda behind them, so I left them out. No page stated any selfie stick or tripod rule, and no page gave a safety point specific to this landmark.
